title.narrative: Scaling Up Nutrition Technical Assistance (SUN TA)

description.narrative: (Zambia): .The Scaling Up Nutrition Technical Assistance activity works through the Zambian government to reduce stunting among children under age two in 13 national districts. It aims to address the drivers of stunting including: 1) inadequate dietary diversity among women and children; 2) achieving minimally acceptable diets for children under two years of age; 3) promoting health-seeking behaviors including family planning, maternal and child health; and 4) increasing access to safe drinking water and improved sanitation. With FY 2022 funds, USAID will provide technical assistance to strengthen the delivery of high-priority maternal child health interventions that will lower the rates of diarrheal illness and improve appropriate management of diarrhea, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, and agriculture interventions to reduce stunting. The activity will support households with pregnant and lactating women through Social Behavior Change interventions, and family planning training and commodities to communities to expand access to family planning services and promotion of contraceptive use. Further, the funds will support counseling on maternal and/or child nutrition. District and village level Water Sanitation and Hygiene champions will be trained to improve sanitation and access to safe water, new wells will be drilled and old ones will be rehabilitated. The activity will promote household food security by supporting contract farming with private sector partners. Under USAID's CDCS, the mechanism will support Development Objective 2: Rural Poverty Reduced through Enterprise-Driven, Inclusive Economic Growth, and Development Objective 3: Capacity of Zambia's Government, Citizens and Private Sector Increased to Improve Health Outcomes and Meet Critical Needs of Vulnerable Populations. This mechanism contributes directly to the Administration's policy priority of building global health security capacity by investing in basic health care systems. .
